kernelIdea: z̄ = a − bi. Conjugation undoes itself; Re(z) = (z + z̄)/2, Im(z) = (z − z̄)/(2i), and z·z̄ = a² + b² is real and ≥ 0. z is real iff z = z̄.

kernels.l1: Flip the point across the middle line. Flip it twice and you are home.
kernels.l2: The mirror flips a point across the middle line: the across part stays, the up part goes the other way. Points sitting on the line do not move at all.
kernels.l3: The conjugate of a + bi is a − bi — the mirror image across the horizontal line. Doing it twice gets you back, and a number equals its own conjugate exactly when it is an ordinary number.
kernels.l4: The conjugate of z = a + bi is z̄ = a − bi. Conjugation undoes itself, Re(z) = (z + z̄)/2, Im(z) = (z − z̄)/(2i), and z z̄ = a² + b² ≥ 0 is real. z is real iff z = z̄.
kernels.l5: Conjugation is a reflection in the real axis that respects sums and products; z z̄ is real and non-negative, and its fixed points are exactly the reals.
kernels.l6: Conjugation respects sums and products and leaves every real number where it is; the numbers it fixes are exactly the reals, so no algebraic property distinguishes i from −i.
kernels.l7: Conjugation respects sums and products, is its own inverse, and fixes exactly the reals. A number times its conjugate is real and non-negative, and the two parts are recoverable from the number and its conjugate.
kernels.l8: Conjugation generates Gal(ℂ/ℝ) ≅ ℤ/2ℤ; the conjugate-root theorem for real polynomials is an immediate consequence of its being a ring homomorphism.
